findings.title: Unexplained Medicare eligibility under 65
findings.observed: 51 patients have Medicare, and 32 of them are under 65 (min age 18, median 37).
findings.expected: Medicare is a federal health insurance program primarily for individuals aged 65 or older. Younger individuals may qualify through disability, but 32% of the panel having this status is unusual.
findings.impact: Incorrectly assigned insurance would break any analysis of cost or utilisation, and cohort screening on payer would be entirely wrong.

findings.title: Extremely high rate of PCSK9 inhibitor prescribing
findings.observed: 16 of 100 patients are on a PCSK9 inhibitor, a rate several hundred times higher than in any general-practice population.
findings.expected: PCSK9 inhibitors are third-line agents for refractory hyperlipidaemia, used by a fraction of a percent of a general primary-care population.
findings.impact: An algorithm built on this data would inherit a massive bias in prescribing patterns. If this is a specialised population, any rule for primary care would be wrong; if it is meant to be primary care, the panel is unrepresentative.
findings.plausible_if: a lipid-apheresis unit or a clinic for refractory dyslipidaemia

findings.title: Apparent duplicate therapy is an artifact of missing discontinuation data
findings.observed: 20 patients are on more than one agent of the same class, but the start dates are 113 to 1376 days apart (mean 814), and not one of the 522 medication orders in the extract has a stop date.
findings.expected: A patient switching from one agent to another should have the first one recorded as discontinued. All 522 orders in this extract are marked 'Active'.
findings.impact: Any algorithm trying to spot duplicate therapy, measure adherence or assess costs will be wrong. These 20 cases look like double or triple therapy but are almost certainly switches with no stop date recorded.

findings.title: Implausible reference ranges
findings.observed: 9 analytes have a reference range that starts at 0.
findings.expected: A laboratory does not report a reference range of 0 for cholesterol, triglycerides, or BNP.
findings.impact: A reference range of 0 makes it impossible to flag results that are too low. It also explains the implausibly low values seen in the results -- a distribution drawn across [0, upper] will run down to nothing.
findings.affected: BNP, H. pylori Ag Stool, IgE Total, LDL Cholesterol, Lipid Panel — Total Chol, NT-proBNP, Total Cholesterol, Triglycerides, Urine Albumin/Creat Ratio

findings.title: SpO2 above 100%
findings.impact: This value is physiologically impossible and would be filtered out by any clinical rule, but its presence suggests a problem with the data collection or recording process.

findings.title: Sodium levels incompatible with life
findings.observed: 14 of 56 sodium results are above the physiologic maximum of 160 mEq/L, with a maximum value of 209.91 mEq/L.
findings.expected: The physiologic limit for sodium is 160 mEq/L. Values above this are incompatible with life.
findings.impact: These sodium levels are fatally high. No clinical algorithm can run on this data without extensive filtering. This points to a severe data integrity issue.

findings.title: Hemoglobin levels incompatible with life
findings.observed: 4 of 43 hemoglobin results are above the physiologic maximum of 22 g/dL, with a maximum value of 25.12 g/dL.
findings.expected: The physiologic limit for hemoglobin is 22 g/dL.
findings.impact: These hemoglobin levels are physiologically impossible and suggest a problem with the lab instrument or data entry. Clinical decisions based on this data would be dangerously wrong.

findings.title: eGFR values are not physiologically plausible
findings.observed: 8 of 84 eGFR results are above the plausible maximum of 150, with a maximum value of 172.95.
findings.expected: The plausible limit for eGFR is 150 mL/min/1.73m2. While hyperfiltration exists, values beyond this are not credible.
findings.impact: An eGFR of 173 is not a kidney. These values would be rejected by any clinical algorithm and point to a data quality problem.

findings.title: Implausibly low total cholesterol
findings.observed: 17 of 50 (34%) total cholesterol results are under 50 mg/dL, with a minimum of 7.08 mg/dL.
findings.expected: Total cholesterol below 50 mg/dL is physiologically implausible.
findings.impact: A third of the total cholesterol results are not believable. This is likely related to the finding that the reference range for this analyte is incorrectly anchored at 0. No lipid-based risk score can be computed on this data.

findings.title: Implausibly low LDL cholesterol
findings.observed: 3 of 72 (4%) LDL cholesterol results are under 10 mg/dL, with a minimum of 0.13 mg/dL.
findings.expected: LDL cholesterol below 10 mg/dL is physiologically implausible.
findings.impact: These LDL values are not believable and are likely the result of the reference range being incorrectly anchored at 0. Lipid-based risk calculations would be invalid.

verdict:
This EHR extract has severe and wide-ranging data quality problems that make it unsafe for building clinical logic. The issues fall into all three categories of plausibility problems:

**Impossible values:** The dataset contains numerous physiologically impossible lab results. These include an SpO2 reading of 126%, sodium levels as high as 209.91 mEq/L, and hemoglobin up to 25.12 g/dL. Additionally, a large portion of the cholesterol results are implausibly low (34% of total cholesterol results are under 50 mg/dL), which is likely a result of incorrect reference ranges. These are not isolated errors and point to a systemic problem with data recording or extraction.

**Internal inconsistencies:** The extract has fundamental structural problems. None of the 522 medication orders have discontinuation dates, meaning that medication switches appear as dangerous duplicate therapy. Furthermore, a large number of patients under 65 are listed as having Medicare, which is not typical and suggests a systematic error in assigning insurance data. Nine lab analytes have implausible reference ranges starting from zero, which corrupts the interpretation of the results.

**Population-dependent findings:** The prescribing rates suggest a highly specialized patient population. For instance, 16% of patients are on PCSK9 inhibitors, a rate that would be extraordinary in a general population but plausible in a specialized lipid clinic. Without knowing the origin of this data, any clinical logic built upon it would be dangerously biased.

**Verdict:** This extract is not safe to build clinical logic on. The impossible lab values and missing medication data alone would create dangerously incorrect outputs. The population characteristics are so unusual that any model trained on this data would not be generalizable. Before this data can be used, the owner must clarify the origin of the panel, and the impossible and inconsistent data must be investigated and corrected at the source.
